chapter_text:
CHAPTER 30 — HUMAN IMPACT ON ENVIRONMENT

Introduction

Human beings are part of the environment, yet no other species has changed it as profoundly. Farming, industry, transport, mining and the building of towns and cities have given us comfort and prosperity, but they have also disturbed the delicate balance of the natural world. As the human population has grown from about one billion in 1800 to more than eight billion today, the demand for food, water, energy and raw materials has multiplied many times over. The result is widespread POLLUTION, the loss of forests and wildlife, the warming of the planet, the thinning of the protective ozone layer and the steady erosion of soil and fresh water. This chapter examines how human activities damage the environment and what we can do, as individuals and as a society, to repair and protect it.

30.1 POLLUTION

Pollution is any undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological properties of air, water or soil that harms living things. The substance that causes pollution is called a POLLUTANT. Pollutants may be non-biodegradable (such as plastics, DDT and many metals) which persist for a long time, or biodegradable (such as sewage and food waste) which are broken down by microorganisms.

(a) Air pollution. The burning of fossil fuels (coal, petrol, diesel) in vehicles, power stations and factories releases carbon dioxide (CO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO2), oxides of nitrogen (NOx) and tiny particles of soot and dust. Effects include respiratory diseases such as asthma and bronchitis, smog over cities, damage to plants, acid rain and the greenhouse effect. The Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984, in which methyl isocyanate leaked from a factory, is a grim reminder of how dangerous air pollution can be.

(b) Water pollution. Untreated sewage, industrial effluents, fertilisers and pesticides washed from farms, and oil spills all foul our rivers, lakes and seas. Fertiliser run-off causes EUTROPHICATION: nutrients make algae grow rapidly (an algal bloom); when the algae die and decay, the dissolved oxygen in the water is used up, killing fish and other aquatic life. Sewage spreads diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery. Non-biodegradable pollutants such as mercury and DDT undergo BIOMAGNIFICATION, becoming more concentrated as they pass up the food chain.

(c) Soil pollution. The over-use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, dumping of solid waste and industrial chemicals, and acid rain reduce soil fertility, kill useful soil organisms and contaminate crops.

(d) Noise pollution. Unwanted, loud sound from traffic, factories, loudspeakers and machinery (measured in decibels, dB) causes loss of hearing, high blood pressure, sleeplessness and stress.

30.2 DEFORESTATION

Deforestation is the large-scale cutting down and clearing of forests. Its main causes are: clearing land for AGRICULTURE; URBANISATION (building houses, roads and factories); commercial LOGGING for timber, paper and fuel-wood; and MINING. The consequences are serious:

- SOIL EROSION: tree roots bind the soil; without them, wind and rain wash away the fertile topsoil, leading to desertification.
- LOSS OF BIODIVERSITY: forests are home to most land species; clearing them destroys habitats and pushes plants and animals towards extinction.
- CLIMATE CHANGE: trees absorb CO2 during photosynthesis; fewer trees means more CO2 in the air, adding to global warming.
- FLOODS AND DROUGHTS: forests slow rainfall run-off and help the ground hold water. Their loss causes floods in the rainy season and droughts in the dry season, and lowers the water table.
- DISTURBED WATER CYCLE: forests release water vapour by transpiration and help bring rain; deforestation reduces rainfall.

30.3 GLOBAL WARMING AND THE GREENHOUSE EFFECT

The Earth is kept warm by the GREENHOUSE EFFECT. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface; the warm surface radiates heat back as infrared rays. Certain gases in the atmosphere — the GREENHOUSE GASES — trap part of this heat, just as the glass of a greenhouse traps warmth, keeping the planet about 33 degrees C warmer than it would otherwise be. The main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), water vapour and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).

Human activities — burning fossil fuels, deforestation, intensive farming and cattle rearing — have raised the concentration of these gases sharply. The extra trapped heat is causing GLOBAL WARMING: a steady rise in the Earth's average temperature. Its consequences include:

- Melting of glaciers and polar ice caps.
- A rise in sea level, threatening to drown low-lying islands and coastal cities.
- More frequent and severe extreme weather — floods, droughts, cyclones and heat waves.
- Shifting rainfall patterns that harm agriculture.
- Spread of diseases and loss of species unable to adapt.

International agreements such as the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) aim to cut greenhouse-gas emissions.

30.4 OZONE LAYER DEPLETION

High up in the stratosphere, a layer of OZONE (O3) absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ULTRAVIOLET (UV) radiation, acting as a shield for life on Earth. CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS (CFCs) — once widely used in refrigerators, air-conditioners, aerosol sprays and foam — drift up to the stratosphere where UV light breaks them apart, releasing chlorine atoms. Each chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. This has thinned the ozone layer and created the OZONE HOLE over Antarctica.

The harmful effects of increased UV radiation include skin cancer, cataracts (clouding of the eye lens), weakening of the immune system, and damage to crops and to the tiny plankton that form the base of ocean food chains. To tackle this, the world signed the MONTREAL PROTOCOL (1987), which has successfully phased out CFCs; the ozone layer is now slowly recovering.

30.5 ACID RAIN

When sulphur dioxide (SO2) and oxides of nitrogen (NOx) — released by burning fossil fuels — dissolve in atmospheric moisture, they form sulphuric and nitric acids. These fall to the ground as ACID RAIN (rain with a pH below 5.6). Acid rain damages buildings and monuments (the Taj Mahal has suffered), corrodes metals, kills fish by acidifying lakes and rivers, harms forests, and leaches nutrients from the soil.

30.6 LOSS OF BIODIVERSITY AND EXTINCTION

BIODIVERSITY is the variety of all living organisms — the different species of plants, animals and microbes and the ecosystems they form. It gives us food, medicines, timber and clean air and water, and keeps ecosystems stable. Habitat destruction, pollution, over-hunting, over-fishing and the introduction of foreign (invasive) species are driving many organisms to EXTINCTION (the complete disappearance of a species). Animals such as the dodo and the cheetah (in India) have already been lost; the tiger, the great Indian bustard and many others are ENDANGERED. India is one of the world's twelve mega-biodiversity countries, with several biodiversity hotspots such as the Western Ghats and the Eastern Himalayas.

30.7 MANAGEMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES AND THE THREE R's

NATURAL RESOURCES (forests, water, soil, minerals, fossil fuels, wildlife) must be used wisely so that they are not exhausted. Resources are RENEWABLE (replenished by nature, such as forests, water and solar energy) or NON-RENEWABLE (limited and not replaced in our lifetime, such as coal, petroleum and minerals).

A simple guiding principle is the THREE R's:
- REDUCE: use less — switch off unused lights and taps, avoid wasteful packaging, save fuel.
- REUSE: use things again instead of throwing them away — refill bottles, use cloth bags, repair rather than replace.
- RECYCLE: collect used materials such as paper, glass, metals and plastics and process them into new products, saving raw materials and energy.

SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT means meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It balances economic growth with the conservation of resources and the protection of the environment.

30.8 CONSERVATION OF FORESTS AND WILDLIFE

Forests are conserved through afforestation (planting trees), reforestation, controlled grazing and a ban on illegal felling. To protect wildlife, India has set up:
- NATIONAL PARKS (e.g. Jim Corbett, Kaziranga) — strictly protected areas where no human activity such as grazing or farming is allowed.
- WILDLIFE SANCTUARIES — protected areas where some human activities are permitted but hunting is banned.
- BIOSPHERE RESERVES (e.g. Nilgiri, Sundarbans) — large areas that conserve whole ecosystems along with their plants, animals and the traditional lifestyles of local people.

PROJECT TIGER, launched in 1973, created tiger reserves to save the dwindling tiger population. The CHIPKO MOVEMENT (1970s, led by villagers including Sunderlal Bahuguna and women of the Garhwal Himalayas) is a famous example of people hugging trees to stop them being cut — a powerful symbol of community conservation. Laws such as the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 protect India's natural heritage.

30.9 CONSERVATION OF WATER AND SOIL

Fresh water is scarce and precious. It is conserved by RAINWATER HARVESTING (collecting and storing rainwater), building check-dams, recharging groundwater, preventing leakage, recycling water and using drip irrigation that delivers water directly to plant roots. Watershed management protects whole drainage areas.

Soil is conserved by preventing erosion: contour ploughing (ploughing along the slope), terrace farming on hillsides, planting trees and grass (shelter belts) to bind the soil and break the wind, crop rotation, and adding organic manure to keep the soil fertile.

30.10 WASTE MANAGEMENT

The huge quantities of waste we produce must be handled carefully. Wastes are sorted into BIODEGRADABLE (vegetable peels, paper — turned into compost) and NON-BIODEGRADABLE (plastics, glass, metals — sent for recycling). Proper waste management includes segregation at source, composting, recycling, sanitary landfills and the safe treatment of sewage and hazardous industrial and electronic (e-) waste.

30.11 RENEWABLE ENERGY

Replacing fossil fuels with clean RENEWABLE ENERGY reduces pollution and greenhouse gases. Renewable sources include solar energy (solar cells and solar heaters), wind energy (windmills), hydro (water) power, tidal energy, geothermal energy and biogas/biomass. These sources do not run out and cause far less pollution than coal or oil.

30.12 ROLE OF THE INDIVIDUAL

Protecting the environment is everyone's duty. Each of us can: save electricity and water; use public transport, cycling or walking; plant and care for trees; carry cloth bags and refuse single-use plastics; segregate waste and compost kitchen scraps; reduce, reuse and recycle; and spread awareness. Small actions by millions of people add up to a large difference.

SUMMARY

- Human activities — farming, industry, transport, mining and urbanisation — have disturbed the natural balance of the environment.
- Pollution of air, water, soil and by noise harms health and ecosystems; pollutants may be biodegradable or non-biodegradable.
- Deforestation causes soil erosion, loss of biodiversity, climate change and floods/droughts.
- The greenhouse effect, intensified by greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs), is causing global warming, melting glaciers and sea-level rise.
- CFCs deplete the protective ozone layer, increasing harmful UV radiation; the Montreal Protocol is helping it recover.
- Acid rain, from SO2 and NOx, damages life, soil, water and monuments.
- Biodiversity is being lost through habitat destruction and over-exploitation, driving species to extinction.
- Natural resources must be managed by the three R's (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) and the principle of sustainable development.
- Forests and wildlife are conserved through national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, Project Tiger and movements such as Chipko.
- Water and soil are conserved by rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation, contour and terrace farming, and afforestation; renewable energy and responsible individual action protect the environment for the future.

chapter_summary.title: Human Impact on Environment — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 30 explains how human activities pollute the air, water and soil, drive deforestation, warm the planet, deplete the ozone layer and cause acid rain and loss of biodiversity, and sets out how we conserve forests, wildlife, water and soil through the three R's and sustainable development.

sections.heading: Pollution and its types
bullets: Pollution is any undesirable change in the air, water or soil that harms living things; the agent is called a pollutant.
Air pollution from burning fossil fuels releases CO2, CO, SO2 and NOx, causing respiratory disease, smog, acid rain and the greenhouse effect.
Water pollution from sewage and fertiliser run-off spreads disease and causes eutrophication (algal blooms that remove oxygen).
Pollutants may be biodegradable (broken down by microbes) or non-biodegradable (persist and may biomagnify up the food chain); noise pollution harms hearing and health.

sections.heading: Deforestation
bullets: Deforestation is the large-scale clearing of forests for agriculture, urbanisation, logging and mining.
It causes soil erosion and loss of fertile topsoil because tree roots no longer bind the soil.
It destroys habitats, reducing biodiversity, and removes trees that absorb CO2, adding to climate change.
It disturbs the water cycle, causing floods and droughts and lowering the water table.

sections.heading: Global warming, ozone depletion and acid rain
bullets: Greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs) trap heat; rising levels cause global warming, melting glaciers, sea-level rise and extreme weather.
CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone, creating the ozone hole and letting in harmful UV that causes skin cancer and cataracts; the Montreal Protocol (1987) is helping recovery.
Acid rain forms when SO2 and NOx dissolve in rain water, damaging buildings, forests, soil and aquatic life.

sections.heading: Conservation of natural resources
bullets: Natural resources are renewable (forests, water, solar) or non-renewable (coal, petroleum, minerals) and must be used wisely.
The three R's — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle — cut waste and save raw materials and energy.
Sustainable development meets present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
Renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro, biogas) and good waste management reduce pollution and greenhouse gases.

sections.heading: Conservation of forests, wildlife, water and soil
bullets: Biodiversity gives us food, medicine and stable ecosystems; habitat loss and over-exploitation drive species to extinction.
Wildlife is protected in national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves, and by Project Tiger and the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
The Chipko movement is a famous example of community-led forest conservation.
Water is saved by rainwater harvesting and drip irrigation; soil is saved by contour ploughing, terrace farming and afforestation.

key_takeaways: Human activities pollute air, water and soil and create noise pollution, harming health and ecosystems.
Deforestation causes soil erosion, loss of biodiversity, climate change and floods or droughts.
Greenhouse gases cause global warming, melting glaciers and sea-level rise; CFCs deplete the ozone layer.
Acid rain from SO2 and NOx damages life, soil, water and monuments such as the Taj Mahal.
The three R's (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) and sustainable development help conserve limited natural resources.
Forests and wildlife are conserved by national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, Project Tiger and the Chipko movement.
Every individual can help by saving water and energy, planting trees, refusing plastics and managing waste.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Human Impact on Environment (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-30 for Lesson 30. Attempt all questions. Support your answers with examples wherever possible.

questions.question: What is pollution? Name the four main types of pollution.
questions.answer: Pollution is any undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological properties of air, water or soil that harms living things. The four main types are: (1) AIR pollution, (2) WATER pollution, (3) SOIL (land) pollution, and (4) NOISE pollution.
questions.explanation: Definition plus the four standard categories.

questions.question: Distinguish between biodegradable and non-biodegradable pollutants, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: BIODEGRADABLE pollutants can be broken down by microorganisms into simpler, harmless substances. Example: sewage or vegetable waste. NON-BIODEGRADABLE pollutants cannot be broken down by microbes and persist in the environment for a very long time. Example: plastics, DDT or mercury. Non-biodegradable pollutants are dangerous because they accumulate and may undergo biomagnification up the food chain.

questions.question: Explain the causes and consequences of deforestation.
questions.answer:
CAUSES of deforestation: (1) clearing land for AGRICULTURE to feed the growing population; (2) URBANISATION — building houses, roads, dams and factories; (3) commercial LOGGING for timber, paper and fuel-wood; and (4) MINING for minerals.

CONSEQUENCES: (1) SOIL EROSION — without tree roots to bind it, fertile topsoil is washed or blown away, leading to desertification. (2) LOSS OF BIODIVERSITY — forests are home to most land species, so clearing them destroys habitats and causes extinction. (3) CLIMATE CHANGE — fewer trees means less CO2 is absorbed, so more remains in the air, adding to global warming. (4) FLOODS AND DROUGHTS — forests slow run-off and store water; their loss causes floods in the wet season, droughts in the dry season and a falling water table. (5) DISTURBED WATER CYCLE and reduced rainfall, because forests release water vapour by transpiration.
questions.explanation: Four causes and several consequences with reasons.

questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect? Name two greenhouse gases.
questions.answer: The greenhouse effect is the trapping of the Earth's outgoing infrared heat by certain gases in the atmosphere, which keeps the planet warm enough for life (about 33 degrees C warmer than it would otherwise be). Two greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4). (Others include nitrous oxide, water vapour and CFCs.)

questions.question: How is the ozone layer being depleted, and what are the harmful effects of ozone depletion? Name the protocol signed to protect it.
questions.answer:
The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation. CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS (CFCs), once used in refrigerators, air-conditioners and aerosol sprays, drift up to the stratosphere. There, UV light breaks them apart and releases CHLORINE atoms; each chlorine atom destroys thousands of ozone molecules. This thins the ozone layer and has created the OZONE HOLE over Antarctica.

Harmful effects of the increased UV reaching the surface include: skin cancer; cataracts (clouding of the eye lens); weakening of the immune system; and damage to crops and to ocean plankton.

The MONTREAL PROTOCOL (1987) was signed to phase out CFCs, and the ozone layer is now slowly recovering.
questions.explanation: Mechanism, effects, and the Montreal Protocol.

questions.question: What is acid rain? State two of its harmful effects.
questions.answer: Acid rain is rain made acidic (pH below 5.6) when sulphur dioxide (SO2) and oxides of nitrogen (NOx) from burning fossil fuels dissolve in atmospheric moisture to form sulphuric and nitric acids. Two harmful effects: (1) it damages buildings and monuments (for example the Taj Mahal) and corrodes metals; (2) it acidifies lakes and rivers, killing fish and other aquatic life. It also harms forests and leaches nutrients from soil.

questions.question: What are the three R's of waste management? Explain each briefly.
questions.answer: The three R's are REDUCE, REUSE and RECYCLE. REDUCE means using less — for example switching off unused lights and taps and avoiding wasteful packaging. REUSE means using things again instead of throwing them away — for example refilling bottles or using cloth bags. RECYCLE means processing used materials such as paper, glass, metals and plastics into new products, saving raw materials and energy.
questions.explanation: Name and explain each of the three R's.

questions.question: Differentiate between a national park and a wildlife sanctuary.
questions.answer: A NATIONAL PARK is a strictly protected area reserved for the conservation of wildlife and its habitat, where human activities such as grazing, farming and forestry are NOT allowed (e.g. Kaziranga, Jim Corbett). A WILDLIFE SANCTUARY is a protected area where the focus is protecting particular animal species; some human activities such as grazing or collection of forest produce may be allowed, but hunting is banned. National parks have stricter protection than sanctuaries.
questions.explanation: Compare level of protection and permitted activities.

questions.question: Why is biodiversity important, and what measures can be taken to conserve forests and wildlife?
questions.answer:
IMPORTANCE OF BIODIVERSITY: it provides food, medicines, timber, fibres and clean air and water; it keeps ecosystems stable and resilient; and it maintains the natural balance through food chains and webs. Loss of biodiversity through habitat destruction, pollution and over-hunting drives species to extinction.

MEASURES TO CONSERVE FORESTS AND WILDLIFE: afforestation and reforestation (planting trees); a ban on illegal felling and on hunting; setting up NATIONAL PARKS, WILDLIFE SANCTUARIES and BIOSPHERE RESERVES to protect habitats; special programmes such as PROJECT TIGER (1973); laws such as the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; and community efforts such as the CHIPKO MOVEMENT. Captive breeding and seed banks also help conserve endangered species.
questions.explanation: Importance of biodiversity plus conservation measures.

questions.question: List four things an individual can do to protect the environment.
questions.answer: Any four of: (1) save electricity and water by switching off when not in use; (2) use public transport, cycling or walking instead of private vehicles; (3) plant and care for trees; (4) carry cloth bags and refuse single-use plastics; (5) segregate waste and compost kitchen scraps; (6) follow the three R's — reduce, reuse, recycle; (7) spread awareness about the environment.
questions.explanation: Practical individual actions; any four accepted.

questions.question: A substance that causes pollution is called a ____.
Excessive growth of algae due to nutrient run-off is called ____.
The increase in concentration of a toxin up a food chain is called ____.
The large-scale clearing of forests is called ____.
Loss of fertile topsoil due to wind and water is called soil ____.
The trapping of the Earth's heat by atmospheric gases is the ____ effect.
Melting of glaciers due to global warming causes a rise in ____ level.
The gas that forms the protective layer in the stratosphere is ____.
Ozone depletion is mainly caused by ____.
Rain made acidic by SO2 and NOx is called ____.
The three R's are Reduce, Reuse and ____.
Development that does not harm future generations is called ____ development.
Collecting and storing rainwater is called rainwater ____.
The movement in which people hugged trees to save them was the ____ movement.
questions.explanation: Led by Himalayan villagers in the 1970s.

questions.question: The variety of all living organisms is called ____.
Name the four main types of pollution.
questions.answer: The four main types of pollution are: (1) AIR pollution, (2) WATER pollution, (3) SOIL (land) pollution, and (4) NOISE pollution.

questions.question: What is eutrophication and why is it harmful?
questions.answer: Eutrophication is the excessive growth of algae in a water body caused by nutrients (from fertiliser run-off and sewage). It is harmful because when the dense algae die and decay, microbes use up the dissolved oxygen in the water, leaving too little for fish and other aquatic life, which then die.

questions.question: List two harmful effects of air pollution on human health.
questions.answer: Two harmful effects: (1) respiratory diseases such as asthma and bronchitis caused by smoke, dust and gases; (2) irritation of the eyes and lungs, and over time more serious illnesses, from breathing polluted, smoggy air.

questions.question: Explain biomagnification with an example.
questions.answer: Biomagnification is the increase in the concentration of a non-biodegradable pollutant as it moves up a food chain. For example, DDT sprayed on crops washes into water and is taken up by tiny plankton in very small amounts. Small fish eat many plankton, large fish eat many small fish, and birds eat many large fish. At each step the DDT becomes more concentrated, so top predators (and humans) end up with dangerously high levels even though the water itself had only a little.

questions.question: What is noise pollution and name one of its effects?
questions.answer: Noise pollution is unwanted, excessively loud sound (measured in decibels) from traffic, machinery and loudspeakers. One effect is loss of hearing; it also causes high blood pressure, sleeplessness and stress.

questions.question: State two causes of deforestation.
questions.answer: Two causes of deforestation are: (1) clearing land for AGRICULTURE; and (2) cutting trees for URBANISATION (building houses, roads and factories). Other causes include logging for timber and fuel-wood, and mining.

questions.question: How does deforestation lead to soil erosion and floods?
questions.answer: Tree roots normally bind the soil and the canopy slows falling rain, while leaf litter helps the ground soak up water. When forests are cleared, there are no roots to hold the soil, so wind and rain wash away the fertile topsoil — this is SOIL EROSION. The bare ground also cannot absorb rainwater, so during heavy rain the water rushes off the surface into rivers all at once, causing FLOODS (and in the dry season, droughts, as little water is stored).

questions.question: How does deforestation contribute to global warming?
questions.answer: Trees absorb carbon dioxide from the air during photosynthesis and store the carbon in wood. When forests are cut down and burned, this stored carbon is released as CO2, and fewer trees remain to absorb CO2. Both effects raise the level of this greenhouse gas, adding to global warming.

questions.question: Why is deforestation a major cause of loss of biodiversity?
questions.answer: Forests are the natural home (habitat) of the majority of land plants, animals, insects and microorganisms. Many species are adapted to live only in a particular forest and cannot survive elsewhere. When the forest is cleared, these species lose their food, shelter and breeding places. Unable to find another suitable habitat, their numbers fall and many become extinct. Because forests hold such a large share of the world's species, their destruction causes a large loss of biodiversity.

questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?
questions.answer: The greenhouse effect is the trapping of the Earth's outgoing infrared heat by gases such as CO2, methane and water vapour in the atmosphere. These gases let sunlight in but absorb the heat radiated back from the surface, keeping the Earth warm enough (about 33 degrees C warmer) for life to exist.

questions.question: Name four greenhouse gases.
questions.answer: Four greenhouse gases are: carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O) and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). Water vapour is also a greenhouse gas.

questions.question: State three consequences of global warming.
questions.answer: Three consequences of global warming: (1) MELTING of glaciers and polar ice caps; (2) a RISE IN SEA LEVEL that threatens low-lying coastal cities and islands with flooding; and (3) more frequent and severe EXTREME WEATHER such as floods, droughts, cyclones and heat waves. It also shifts rainfall patterns and harms crops and wildlife.

questions.question: How do human activities increase the greenhouse effect?
questions.answer: Human activities raise the levels of greenhouse gases. Burning fossil fuels (coal, petrol, diesel) in vehicles, factories and power stations releases large amounts of CO2. Deforestation removes trees that would absorb CO2. Cattle rearing and paddy farming release methane, and use of fertilisers releases nitrous oxide. More greenhouse gases trap more heat, intensifying the greenhouse effect and causing global warming.
questions.explanation: Emissions plus loss of CO2 sinks.

questions.question: What is the function of the ozone layer?
questions.answer: The ozone layer, found in the stratosphere, absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation before it reaches the Earth's surface. It thus acts as a protective shield for living things, preventing damage such as skin cancer, cataracts and harm to crops.

questions.question: Explain how CFCs cause ozone depletion.
questions.answer: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), released from refrigerators, air-conditioners and aerosol sprays, are very stable and slowly rise to the stratosphere. There, strong ultraviolet light breaks them apart, releasing free CHLORINE atoms. Each chlorine atom reacts with ozone (O3) and breaks it down into ordinary oxygen, and is then freed again to destroy more ozone. In this way one chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules, thinning the ozone layer and creating the ozone hole over Antarctica.
questions.explanation: Chlorine acts as a catalyst destroying ozone.

questions.question: State two harmful effects of increased UV radiation on humans.
questions.answer: Two harmful effects of increased UV radiation: (1) skin cancer; and (2) cataracts (clouding of the lens of the eye). It also weakens the immune system.

questions.question: What is acid rain, how is it formed, and what are its effects?
questions.answer: Acid rain is rain made acidic (pH below about 5.6). It forms when sulphur dioxide (SO2) and oxides of nitrogen (NOx) — released by burning fossil fuels — dissolve in water droplets in the atmosphere to make sulphuric acid and nitric acid, which then fall with the rain. Effects: it damages buildings and monuments (such as the Taj Mahal), corrodes metals, acidifies lakes and rivers and kills fish, harms forests, and leaches nutrients from the soil.

questions.question: Distinguish between global warming and ozone depletion in terms of their causes.
questions.answer: GLOBAL WARMING is caused mainly by GREENHOUSE GASES such as carbon dioxide and methane, which trap the Earth's heat and raise its temperature. OZONE DEPLETION is caused mainly by CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS (CFCs), whose chlorine atoms destroy ozone in the stratosphere and let in more UV radiation. They are two different problems: one is about trapping heat (warming), the other about losing the UV shield (depletion), though both result from human-made pollutants.

questions.question: Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable resources with one example each.
questions.answer: RENEWABLE resources are replaced by nature within a short time and do not run out with careful use — example: solar energy (or forests, water, wind). NON-RENEWABLE resources are limited and are not replaced within a human lifetime — example: coal (or petroleum, natural gas, minerals).

questions.question: Explain the three R's with an everyday example of each.
questions.answer: REDUCE — use less: e.g. switch off lights and fans when leaving a room to save electricity. REUSE — use again instead of discarding: e.g. carry a cloth bag for shopping instead of taking new plastic bags each time. RECYCLE — process waste into new products: e.g. give old newspapers and glass bottles for recycling so they become new paper and glass. Together they cut waste and save raw materials and energy.

questions.question: What is sustainable development?
questions.answer: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It balances economic growth with the conservation of natural resources and protection of the environment, so that resources are not used up or destroyed.

questions.question: Name four sources of renewable energy.
questions.answer: Four sources of renewable energy: (1) solar energy, (2) wind energy, (3) hydro (water) power, and (4) biogas/biomass. Tidal energy and geothermal energy are also renewable sources.

questions.question: Why should we prefer renewable energy over fossil fuels?
questions.answer: Renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro, biogas) should be preferred because: (1) it does not run out — the sources are replenished by nature, unlike limited fossil fuels; (2) it causes far less pollution, releasing little or no carbon dioxide, so it does not add much to global warming or acid rain; and (3) it is available widely and can reduce dependence on imported fuel. Fossil fuels are non-renewable, polluting and a major cause of climate change.

questions.question: What is rainwater harvesting?
questions.answer: Rainwater harvesting is the practice of collecting and storing rainwater — for example in tanks or by directing it into the ground — so that it can be used later and the groundwater is recharged. It is an important way of conserving scarce fresh water.

questions.question: Describe three methods of soil conservation.
questions.answer: Three methods of soil conservation: (1) CONTOUR PLOUGHING — ploughing along the contour lines of a slope so water cannot rush downhill and carry soil away; (2) TERRACE FARMING — making step-like fields on hillsides to reduce the steepness and slow run-off; and (3) PLANTING TREES AND GRASS (afforestation and shelter belts) whose roots bind the soil and whose cover breaks the wind. Crop rotation and adding manure also keep the soil fertile.

questions.question: What is a biosphere reserve?
questions.answer: A biosphere reserve is a large protected area set aside to conserve whole ecosystems — their plants, animals and microorganisms — together with the traditional lifestyles of the local people who live there. Examples in India include the Nilgiri and Sundarbans biosphere reserves.

questions.question: Distinguish between a national park, a wildlife sanctuary and a biosphere reserve.
questions.answer: A NATIONAL PARK is a strictly protected area for wildlife and its habitat where human activities such as grazing and farming are not allowed. A WILDLIFE SANCTUARY protects particular species; hunting is banned but some human activities (such as grazing) may be permitted, so protection is less strict. A BIOSPHERE RESERVE is a very large area that conserves whole ecosystems along with the local human communities and may contain national parks and sanctuaries within it.

questions.question: What is biodiversity and why is it important?
questions.answer: Biodiversity is the variety of all living organisms — the many different species of plants, animals and microbes and the ecosystems they form. It is important because it provides us with food, medicines, timber and clean air and water, and it keeps ecosystems stable and balanced.

questions.question: State three causes of the loss of biodiversity.
questions.answer: Three causes of loss of biodiversity: (1) HABITAT DESTRUCTION through deforestation, mining and urbanisation; (2) POLLUTION of air, water and soil that poisons living things; and (3) OVER-HUNTING and over-fishing of wild species. The introduction of invasive (foreign) species also drives native species towards extinction.

questions.question: Suggest two ways a student can reduce waste at home.
questions.answer: Two ways a student can reduce waste: (1) SEGREGATE waste into biodegradable and non-biodegradable, and compost kitchen scraps to make manure; and (2) follow the three R's — reuse items such as bottles and bags and send paper, glass and plastic for recycling instead of throwing them away.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A lake near a town receives untreated sewage and fertiliser-rich water from nearby farms. Soon the lake is covered with a green layer of algae. After some weeks the fish in the lake begin to die.

(i) What is the green layer on the lake called?
(ii) Name the process taking place in the lake.
(iii) Why do the fish die?
(iv) Suggest one way to prevent this.
questions.answer:
(i) The green layer is an ALGAL BLOOM.
(ii) The process is EUTROPHICATION — nutrient enrichment of the water causing rapid algal growth.
(iii) When the algae die, microbes decompose them and use up the dissolved OXYGEN in the water. With too little oxygen left, the fish suffocate and die.
(iv) Prevention: treat sewage before releasing it, and reduce the use of chemical fertilisers (or stop run-off from farms) so excess nutrients do not reach the lake.
questions.explanation: Identify algal bloom, eutrophication, oxygen depletion and prevention.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A hilly region that was once covered with thick forest has been cleared for farming and a new road. Within a few years the villagers notice that the soil is washing away, the wells are drying up, and floods occur during the rains.

(i) Name the human activity responsible.
(ii) Why is the soil washing away?
(iii) Why are the wells drying up?
(iv) Suggest one measure to repair the damage.
questions.answer:
(i) The activity is DEFORESTATION — clearing the forest for farming and a road.
(ii) The soil washes away because the tree roots that bound the soil are gone and there is no canopy to slow the rain, so the fertile topsoil is eroded by wind and water.
(iii) The wells dry up because, without forest, less rainwater soaks into the ground; more rushes off the surface, so the groundwater (water table) is not recharged and falls.
(iv) Measure: AFFORESTATION (planting trees) along with terrace farming and contour ploughing to bind the soil and help water soak in.
questions.explanation: Link deforestation to erosion, falling water table and remedy.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Scientists report that the Earth's average temperature is rising, glaciers are melting and sea levels are creeping up. They blame increasing amounts of certain gases in the atmosphere produced by burning coal and petroleum.

(i) Name the phenomenon described.
(ii) Name two of the gases responsible.
(iii) State two consequences mentioned.
(iv) Suggest one way to slow it down.
questions.answer:
(i) The phenomenon is GLOBAL WARMING, due to an enhanced greenhouse effect.
(ii) Two responsible gases: carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4). (CFCs and nitrous oxide also contribute.)
(iii) Two consequences mentioned: melting of glaciers and a rise in sea level.
(iv) One way to slow it: reduce the burning of fossil fuels by using renewable energy (solar, wind) and by planting more trees to absorb CO2.
questions.explanation: Identify global warming, gases, consequences, remedy.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A thinning of the ozone layer, with a large 'hole' over Antarctica, has been observed. It is linked to chemicals once used in refrigerators and sprays. As a result, more harmful radiation reaches the Earth.

(i) Which chemicals are responsible?
(ii) Which radiation is the ozone layer supposed to block?
(iii) State one harmful effect of this radiation on humans.
(iv) Name the international protocol signed to solve this problem.
questions.answer:
(i) CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS (CFCs) are responsible.
(ii) The ozone layer blocks harmful ULTRAVIOLET (UV) radiation from the Sun.
(iii) One harmful effect on humans: skin cancer (also cataracts and a weakened immune system).
(iv) The MONTREAL PROTOCOL (1987), which phases out CFCs.
questions.explanation: CFCs, UV, health effect, Montreal Protocol.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In an industrial city with many coal-burning factories, the rain water is found to be acidic. Marble statues in the city are slowly being eaten away and fish are dying in a nearby lake.

(i) What is this acidic rain called?
(ii) Which two gases from the factories cause it?
(iii) Why are the marble statues being damaged?
(iv) Why are the fish dying?
questions.answer:
(i) It is called ACID RAIN.
(ii) The two gases are sulphur dioxide (SO2) and oxides of nitrogen (NOx), which dissolve in rain to form sulphuric and nitric acids.
(iii) The marble (calcium carbonate) reacts with the acid in the rain and is slowly corroded and eaten away.
(iv) The acid rain lowers the pH of the lake water (acidifies it); fish cannot survive in such acidic water, so they die.
questions.explanation: Acid rain, gases, corrosion and acidification.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A school decides to run a 'green campus' project. Students switch off fans and lights not in use, carry tiffin in steel boxes that they wash and use again, and collect paper, bottles and cans to send to a recycling centre.

(i) Which of the three R's is shown by switching off lights?
(ii) Which is shown by reusing steel tiffin boxes?
(iii) Which is shown by sending paper and cans to the recycling centre?
(iv) How does this project support sustainable development?
questions.answer:
(i) Switching off lights shows REDUCE (using less electricity).
(ii) Reusing washable steel boxes shows REUSE.
(iii) Sending paper, bottles and cans for processing shows RECYCLE.
(iv) It supports sustainable development because it saves resources (electricity, raw materials) and reduces waste and pollution, meeting present needs while protecting resources for future generations.
questions.explanation: Match actions to the three R's and sustainability.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In the 1970s, villagers in the Garhwal Himalayas hugged trees to stop contractors from cutting them down. Around the same time, the government started a special programme to save the tiger and created strictly protected areas where no farming or grazing is allowed.

(i) Name the movement in which villagers hugged trees.
(ii) Name the programme started to save the tiger.
(iii) What is the name of a strictly protected area where no farming or grazing is allowed?
(iv) Why are such conservation efforts important?
questions.answer:
(i) The CHIPKO MOVEMENT.
(ii) PROJECT TIGER (launched in 1973).
(iii) A NATIONAL PARK.
(iv) Such efforts are important because they protect forests, wildlife habitats and endangered species, preserve biodiversity, and maintain the natural balance that provides us with clean air, water and other resources.
questions.explanation: Chipko, Project Tiger, national park, importance.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A farmer in a dry, hilly area faces water shortage and soil loss. An expert advises him to build small barriers across the streams, to plough along the slope rather than up and down it, and to make step-like fields on the hillside.

(i) What is the purpose of the small barriers across streams?
(ii) What is ploughing along the slope called?
(iii) What are the step-like fields called?
(iv) Name one more way the farmer could save water.
questions.answer:
(i) The small barriers (check dams) store rainwater and help recharge the groundwater, and they slow run-off so soil is not washed away.
(ii) Ploughing along the slope is called CONTOUR PLOUGHING.
(iii) The step-like fields are called TERRACES (terrace farming).
(iv) One more way to save water: rainwater harvesting, or using drip irrigation that delivers water directly to the roots with very little waste.
questions.explanation: Check dams, contour ploughing, terracing, water saving.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A forest is cleared to build a town. Many kinds of birds, insects and small animals that lived only in that forest are no longer seen anywhere. Some of these species had never been found in any other place.

(i) Define biodiversity.
(ii) What has happened to the species found only in that forest?
(iii) What is the disappearance of a species from the Earth called?
(iv) Why is the loss of such species a serious problem?
questions.answer:
(i) Biodiversity is the variety of all living organisms — the different species of plants, animals and microbes and the ecosystems they form.
(ii) The species that lived only in that forest have lost their habitat; unable to live elsewhere, they have died out.
(iii) The disappearance of a species from the Earth is called EXTINCTION.
(iv) It is serious because each extinct species is lost forever; it may have provided food or medicine, and its loss upsets food chains and the balance of the ecosystem, weakening nature's ability to support life.
questions.explanation: Biodiversity, habitat loss, extinction, why it matters.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A family wants to make their home environment-friendly. They are deciding between (a) installing solar panels, (b) throwing all waste into one bin, (c) buying many single-use plastic items, and (d) composting their vegetable peels.

(i) Which of these choices reduce harm to the environment?
(ii) Which choices harm the environment, and why?
(iii) How does composting help?
(iv) How does using solar panels support sustainable development?
questions.answer:
(i) The helpful choices are (a) installing solar panels and (d) composting vegetable peels.
(ii) Harmful choices: (b) throwing all waste into one bin prevents segregation and recycling and sends more waste to landfills; (c) buying single-use plastics creates non-biodegradable waste that pollutes land and water.
(iii) Composting turns biodegradable vegetable peels into useful manure, reducing waste and avoiding the need for chemical fertilisers.
(iv) Solar panels use a renewable, non-polluting source of energy; they cut the use of fossil fuels and greenhouse-gas emissions, conserving resources for future generations — the essence of sustainable development.
